deep.reconstruction:
This is not a Gauss manuscript. It is page 49 of a printed German elementary arithmetic textbook in Fraktur type, bound into the HB.Leiste bundle, which suggests Gauss's school or early-study copy. The only handwriting visible is faint marginal pencil at the left edge (something like '4q', '1/2', 'x'', '=x''). These are most likely offsets or bleed from the facing manuscript leaf, which the previous-page transcription shows contains x', x'' notation. The printed text opens Section 3, 'Von den Proportionen', and runs as follows.

§121 (Definition). A proportion is the equality of two ratios. An arithmetic ratio is determined by its difference and a geometric ratio by its exponent, i.e. its quotient (§5).
- Arithmetic example: 8 − 6 = 12 − 10 (both sides equal 2).
- Geometric example: 8 : 4 = 12 : 6 (both sides equal 2).

§122 (Corollary). Every multiplication or division example, and any two equal fractions, form a geometric proportion: if a/b = c/d then a:b = c:d.

§123. Only the difference or the exponent matters, not the order of the terms. So one may take the second term to be the first plus the difference (arithmetic case), or the first times the exponent (geometric case).
- Arithmetic: if a − b = p − q and b = a + d, then q = p + d, with d of either sign. The general form is a − (a+d) = p − (p+d). The print writes 'a − a + d', meaning a − (a+d).
- Geometric: if b/a = e = q/p, then b = ae and q = pe. The general form is a : ae = p : pe, with e an integer or a fraction.

§124 (Theorem, statement begun here and finished on p. 50).
- In an arithmetic proportion, the sum of the extremes equals the sum of the means: a + (p+d) = (a+d) + p.
- In a geometric proportion, the product of the extremes equals the product of the means: a·pe = ae·p.
- The proof, on the next page, uses only commutativity of addition and multiplication.

The page serves to set up the rule of three, which is developed in §127 on the next page: fourth term = (product of the means)/(first term).
errors: No mathematical errors. The only issue is notational: 'a − a + d = p − p + d' must be read as a − (a+d) = p − (p+d); taken literally without brackets it would mean a different thing (d = d). This is a period printing convention, not an error.
The convention in §121 that d = b − a, so that the arithmetic ratio a − b equals −d, is consistent with §123 (d may be positive or negative).

results.what: Definition of arithmetic and geometric proportion; general forms a − (a+d) = p − (p+d) and a : ae = p : pe
results.modern_name: Equality of differences / equality of ratios (proportion)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Euclid, Elements V/VII; Nicomachus for arithmetic proportion); standard 18th-century textbook material

results.what: Sum of extremes equals sum of means (arithmetic); product of extremes equals product of means (geometric)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a printed elementary arithmetic textbook page on proportions, not Gauss's own work. It contains nothing beyond school-level material, and the only handwriting is faint marginal offset from the facing leaf.

checkable.asserts: The general arithmetic proportion form is an identity.
Sum of extremes equals sum of means in an arithmetic proportion.
Product of extremes equals product of means in the geometric proportion a : ae = p : pe.
Both ratios in a : ae = p : pe have the same exponent e.

transcription_corrections: The page is printed Fraktur text from a textbook, not Gauss's handwriting; the transcription of the printed text is essentially accurate.
'a − a + d = p − p + d' should be understood as a − (a+d) = p − (p+d).

Faint marginal pencil marks at the left edge (roughly '4q', '1/2', 'x'', '=x'') are omitted from the transcription. They appear to be offset or bleed from the facing manuscript leaf, not annotations on this text.
